title: Polymorphic light eruption
summary: The commonest photodermatosis: itchy papules or vesicles on sun-exposed skin hours after the first strong sun of spring or a holiday. Sun protection, short potent steroid bursts and, for severe cases, specialist ‘hardening’ phototherapy.

glance.think: An itchy rash on the V of the neck, forearms and backs of hands hours to a day after early-season sun, settling within days without further exposure.
glance.engine: A delayed immune reaction to a UV-induced skin antigen, with a failure of normal UV immunosuppression; it improves through the summer (‘hardening’).
glance.backbone: Broad-spectrum high-UVA sunscreen, clothing and gradual exposure; potent topical steroid for flares; refer for phototesting or hardening if severe.
glance.never_miss: Lupus (persistent rash, systemic symptoms, positive ANA) and drug photosensitivity.

what: The commonest **idiopathic (primary) photodermatosis**: a recurrent, itchy, non-scarring eruption on sun-exposed skin appearing hours to a couple of days after the first significant sun exposure of spring/summer or of a sunny holiday. Also called polymorphous light eruption or "prickly heat"/"sun allergy" by the public (not true prickly heat — that is miliaria). Affects roughly 10–20% of people in northern Europe; more common in women, onset usually in the teens to 30s; all skin types.
cause: A delayed-type (cell-mediated) immune reaction to a UV-induced skin antigen. Normally UV exposure suppresses skin immunity; in PMLE that **UV-induced immunosuppression fails**, so the newly photo-induced antigen provokes inflammation. **UVA is the main trigger in most patients** (UVB alone in a minority, both in some) — which is why a high-SPF but weak-UVA sunscreen fails (Case 1). Skin "hardens" with repeated exposure, so it is typically worse early in the season and improves through summer. Family history in a proportion.

list: **Itch or burning** often starting within hours (Case 1: 30 minutes); rash within hours to 1–3 days.
Morphology varies between patients but is **usually consistent in one individual**: small papules (commonest), papulovesicles, plaques, targetoid/EM-like lesions, rarely purpuric.
Sites: **V of neck, upper chest, outer arms/forearms, dorsal hands, legs**; face often relatively spared (habitually exposed, hardened).
Resolves over days–2 weeks without scarring **if further sun is avoided**; can spread and persist with continued exposure (Case 1 extension to trunk).
Variant: **juvenile spring eruption** (papulovesicles on helices of ears in boys).

diagnosis: Clinical: timing (first strong sun), photodistribution, recurrent seasonal pattern, normal health. In **severe, atypical or treatment-resistant** cases (Case 1, Q3) specialists consider: **ANA, anti-Ro/La antibodies** (exclude lupus — SCLE can be triggered by sun and by drugs), **porphyrin screen** (exclude erythropoietic protoporphyria/other porphyrias), skin biopsy (dermal oedema, perivascular lymphocytes — non-specific but helps exclude lupus), and **phototesting/provocation testing** in a photobiology unit. Always take a full drug history to exclude drug-induced photosensitivity.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Uniform painful erythema; no papules; dose-related; within hours, peaks 24 h
New photosensitiser (doxycycline, thiazide, NSAID…); "exaggerated sunburn" or eczema; ask about drugs
Persistent annular/psoriasiform or scarring plaques; ANA/Ro positive; lasts weeks–months
Wheals within **minutes** of exposure, fade within hours
Childhood onset, excoriated papules/nodules incl. covered sites, cheilitis, persists into winter
Targets on palms/soles; HSV/drug trigger; not photodistributed
Eczematous, chronic; shaded sites involved (airborne) or older man, lichenified (CAD)

list: Avoid further sun until settled; cool showers/compresses, emollient.
**Oral non-sedating antihistamine** for itch (helps itch, not the rash) — hydroxyzine in Case 1 had limited effect.
OTC hydrocortisone 1% is usually too weak for established PMLE on limbs/trunk.

**Short course (5–7 days, up to ~2 weeks) of a potent topical corticosteroid** (e.g. betamethasone valerate 0.1%, mometasone 0.1%) to the trunk/limbs; avoid potent on face — use moderate for ≤5–7 days if needed.

Severe extensive flares: a **short course of oral prednisolone** may be used (GP/specialist decision; e.g. a few days at the start of a holiday is a recognised specialist strategy for predictable attacks).
Graded, gradual sun exposure in spring ("natural hardening").
**Broad-spectrum SPF 30–50+ with high UVA protection (UK 4–5 star UVA or EU "UVA" circle logo)**, applied generously 15–30 min before going out and re-applied every 2 h and after swimming.
Clothing, hat, shade, avoid 11:00–15:00; UVA passes through glass (car side windows, conservatory).
Severe recurrent: **referral for prophylactic phototherapy ("hardening") with narrowband UVB or PUVA in spring**; hydroxychloroquine or immunosuppressants are rarely used (specialist).

management: Diagnostic doubt (rule out lupus/porphyria), scarring, persistent >2–3 weeks without sun, systemic features, failure of potent topical steroid, severe recurrent PMLE affecting quality of life (phototherapy referral).
Tutor emphasis (Case 1): **SPF is not the only measure of sunscreen quality** — choose by UVA protection too.

head: Parameter
What to advise
rows: **UK star rating 4–5 stars** (Boots scale) or **EU "UVA" circle logo** (UVA-PF ≥ ⅓ of SPF). Critical — UVA drives PMLE (~75% UVA-induced), drug phototoxicity, phytophotodermatitis, CAD
Chemical filters inadequate — **mineral (titanium dioxide/zinc oxide) tinted/iron-oxide sunscreens**; Dundee cream via specialists
Water-resistant if swimming/sweating, but **re-apply after towelling**
Fragrance-free and minimal-filter for CAD / photoallergy (avoid benzophenone/oxybenzone, octocrylene if allergic — especially with topical ketoprofen history); sprays/gels for hairy skin
~**2 mg/cm²** — about **6 teaspoons (~35 ml)** for an adult whole body; most people apply a third to half of this
Apply 15–30 min before going out; **re-apply every 2 hours** and after swimming/sweating
Avoid **11:00–15:00** in UK summer (sun strongest); UV index ≥3 needs protection; cloud doesn't block UVA
**UVA passes through window glass** — car side windows, conservatories, office windows; UV-filter window film helps (PCT, CAD, drug photosensitivity)
Tightly woven/UPF 50+ clothing, long sleeves, collars, **wide-brimmed hat**, UV-protective sunglasses, gloves for driving (PCT/CAD)
Strict photoprotection → **10 micrograms (400 units) colecalciferol daily** (UK advice), or check levels
Check expiry (usually 12 months after opening); store cool
Sunscreens are **ACBS-approved** on FP10 for *genetic disorders/photodermatoses* (e.g. PMLE, PCT, CAD, porphyrias) — endorse "ACBS"; otherwise self-care purchase

red_flags.h: Photodermatoses: red flags and when to refer

head: Situation
Action
rows: Widespread blistering, mucosal involvement, fever/unwell after new drug
Extensive phytophotodermatitis/hogweed burns, eye involvement, hand/face/genital blisters
Same-day urgent care / burns or eye service
Blisters + fragility + scars/milia on dorsal hands (± alcohol, hep C, oestrogen, iron)
Refer dermatology; urine/plasma porphyrins, LFT, ferritin, hep C/HIV; stop iron/oestrogen review/alcohol
Acute porphyria features (abdominal pain, neuropathy, confusion, hyponatraemia)
**Urgent** medical assessment; check porphyria-safe drug lists
Chronic lichenified photo-distributed eczema in older adult
PMLE not responding to potent topical steroid, scarring, persisting >3 weeks without sun, lupus features
Photosensitivity on essential drug (amiodarone, voriconazole, oncology, HIV)
Don't stop — photoprotect; liaise with specialist; dermatology skin cancer surveillance for voriconazole/long-term HCTZ with prior NMSC
Persistent photosensitivity after culprit drug stopped
New severe photosensitivity in a young adult with no drug cause
Consider HIV, lupus, porphyria — GP bloods/dermatology
Careful history (plants/limes); safeguarding if history inconsistent

pearls: "It's not an allergy to the sun cream — it's a reaction to UVA the cream didn't block." Check the **UVA rating**, not just SPF (tutor point, Case 1).
Expect recurrence each spring/holiday but often milder later in summer; tends to improve over years.
Vitamin D: if strict sun avoidance, advise 10 micrograms (400 units) daily supplement (UK public health advice).
Always run a quick drug check — a new doxycycline or thiazide changes the diagnosis.
